title: Adaptive prefix bucketing and TTL Autopilot
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood's current per-prefix TTLs and cache-key heuristics are effective but require manual tuning to avoid cost or latency regressions. Teams repeatedly ask for prescriptive, low-risk guidance and automated tuning that preserves SLOs while reducing token spend.

Goal:
Design and implement an adaptive "Autopilot" that groups ("buckets") prefixes by usage fingerprint, proposes conservative TTL and keying changes, and applies them via a staged, observable rollout with automatic rollback triggers. The system should be safe-by-default: prioritize zero-customer-impact changes, provide clear confidence bands for savings estimates, and make manual overrides trivial.

Key requirements:
- Bucket prefixes by access shape (read frequency, sequence-length distribution, burstiness, hit decay) instead of purely by literal prefix to prevent fragmentation-induced regressions.
- Compute TTL suggestions per bucket with a confidence interval and expected cost delta vs baseline.
- Propose cache-key transformations (affix trimming, canonicalization rules) only when collision risk is quantified.
- Staged application: shadow run -> small canary -> rolling ramp -> full apply, with automated safety gates and metric-driven rollback.
- Integrate with Console: per-bucket dashboards, per-change expected vs observed savings, and an "explain" view for recommendations.
- Fail-safe: any change that increases error rate, tail latency, or per-request cost beyond thresholds must instantly revert.

Design notes / approach:
1) Fingerprinting & bucketing: generate a compact usage fingerprint per prefix (time-decayed request histogram, median seq-len, 95p token consumption, unique-client-count) and cluster using a lightweight streaming algorithm (online k-means or HDBSCAN-lite) to keep compute bounded. Buckets are stable over 24h windows and annotated with sample prefixes for audits.

2) Hit-model & economics: for each bucket compute a probabilistic hitcurve using sampled request traces and the current KV cache parameters. Use a bayesian bootstrap to produce a distribution of hit-rate vs TTL. Combine with token-cost model to output expected savings and risk (variance). Present this as: "median expected savings (5-95p)".

3) Conservative autopilot rules: default to conservative percentile (median) TTL suggestion and an additional safety margin based on bucket volatility. For buckets with high burstiness, prefer "sticky" short TTLs unless strong hit evidence exists.

4) Safe apply and rollback orchestration: implement four-phase rollout: dry-simulate (off-line estimator), shadow (collect A/B metrics without serving), canary (1% traffic, 12-24h), ramp (1->25->100 over configurable windows). Safety gates: tail latency, error rate, top-k customer hit-rate delta, cost delta. Gates use both absolute and relative thresholds. If any gate trips, automatic rollback to previous TTL/key rules and an incident marker with root-cause hints.

5) Observability & explainability: each recommendation stores the sample traces, hit-model parameters, and a short human-readable rationale (e.g., "steady 3% cumulative hit beyond 30s -> reduce TTL to 30s saves ~12% token cost"). Console will show before/after counterfactuals and a link to the rolling experiment.

Acceptance criteria:
- Prototype computes bucket-level TTL suggestions and presents median + (5p,95p) saving estimates for a 30-day window on historical traffic.
- Autopilot can run a shadow experiment and surface expected vs observed hitcurves in Console.
- Orchestrator can successfully perform a 1% canary rollout and automatically rollback when a simulated latency gate trips.
- Unit/integration tests cover bucketing stability, hit-model calibration, and rollback triggers.
- Documentation: design doc + runbook + Console UX mockups published.

Planned milestones:
- Design doc & proto (this ticket) -> 2025-02-14 (done)
- Hit-model offline prototype & bucketer -> 2025-02-20
- Shadow framework + Console surfacing -> 2025-02-26
- Canary orchestration & safety gates -> 2025-03-05
- First customer pilot (internal workloads) -> 2025-03-12

Open decisions / trade-offs:
- Clustering algorithm: lightweight online k-means vs HDBSCAN-lite. K-means is predictable and fast; HDBSCAN gives better variable-density buckets but is heavier. We will prototype k-means and evaluate sparseness handling.
- Default conservatism level: how large a safety margin to apply to median suggestion. Proposal: start at +20% conservatism for high-volatility buckets and +10% for medium volatility.
